title: Motivation, Procrastination & Habit Change
description: Start with two introductory modules on the essential ideas and how to reason from evidence. Then practise applying the ideas in a detailed case.

nodes.title: Start here
nodes.body:
People can value a goal and still struggle to start. Understanding the moment they get stuck is often more useful than calling them lazy.

What keeps an intended action from becoming something we actually begin?
nodes.sources: Steel (2007), nature of procrastination; Sirois & Pychyl (2013), procrastination and mood regulation.

nodes.title: What motivation means
nodes.body:
A person's willingness or reason to move towards a goal.

For example: A student wants the placement and has already found the application form.

One important limit: Wanting the result does not guarantee that every step will feel easy.
nodes.sources: Steel (2007), nature of procrastination; Sirois & Pychyl (2013), procrastination and mood regulation.

nodes.title: Find the first concept
nodes.prompt: Consider this example: A student wants the placement and has already found the application form. Which concept is most directly demonstrated, without claiming anything beyond the example?
nodes.explanation: The example most directly supports motivation. A person's willingness or reason to move towards a goal. Wanting the result does not guarantee that every step will feel easy.
nodes.counterexample: Procrastination is not enough to establish laziness or a motivational deficit. Task demands, executive functioning and opportunity can all matter.
nodes.sources: Steel (2007), nature of procrastination; Sirois & Pychyl (2013), procrastination and mood regulation.

lessons.title: First notice what happened
lessons.teach: Read what is said before deciding why anyone said it.
lessons.objective: Apply foundations to observable evidence, uncertainty and proportional decisions.

nodes.title: A situation, not a diagnosis
nodes.body:
Dev has to submit a straightforward form to apply for a placement. He has opened it repeatedly without starting.

You can describe an event accurately while remaining uncertain about why it happened.
nodes.sources: Steel (2007), nature of procrastination; Sirois & Pychyl (2013), procrastination and mood regulation.

nodes.title: Listen before you interpret
nodes.prompt: Follow the four messages. Keep the difference between the words said and their possible meaning in mind.
nodes.explanation: The purpose is to connect the term to what can actually be observed.
nodes.counterexample: Procrastination is not enough to establish laziness or a motivational deficit. Task demands, executive functioning and opportunity can all matter.
nodes.sources: Steel (2007), nature of procrastination; Sirois & Pychyl (2013), procrastination and mood regulation.
nodes.scenario: Dev has to submit a straightforward form to apply for a placement. He has opened it repeatedly without starting.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: I know I need to complete the form, but I keep putting it off.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: What happens when you open it?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: I see the personal statement box and feel stuck.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Do you know what information they're asking for?

checks.prompt: What is the most careful conclusion we can draw from the exchange so far?

options.label: We can describe what each speaker requested, while treating any account of their motives as provisional.
options.feedback: This keeps the distinction between what was said and why it may have been said. The latter requires more evidence.

options.label: We can take the last speaker’s explanation as the main cause, because it is the latest information.
options.feedback: Order of speaking does not determine evidential quality; the earlier words still matter.

options.label: We can give the two speakers’ interpretations equal weight, regardless of which one fits the details.
options.feedback: Plausible alternatives can receive different weights when the observed details support them differently.

options.label: We can infer that one speaker has a stable psychological trait if their response appears defensive.
options.feedback: A single interaction may reflect a situation rather than a trait that persists across settings.

options.label: We can stop analysing the situation because multiple explanations remain logically possible.
options.feedback: Uncertainty is a reason to test explanations, not to abandon reasoning.

checks.explanation: People can be sincere about their experience and still have incomplete explanations of why events happened. Procrastination is not enough to establish laziness or a motivational deficit. Task demands, executive functioning and opportunity can all matter.
checks.counterexample: Procrastination is not enough to establish laziness or a motivational deficit. Task demands, executive functioning and opportunity can all matter.

nodes.title: A description or an assumption?
nodes.prompt: Does the sentence report something we can check, or interpret what it might mean?
nodes.explanation: The spoken words are evidence about what was said. A theory of why somebody said them is an interpretation that may need testing.
nodes.counterexample: Procrastination is not enough to establish laziness or a motivational deficit. Task demands, executive functioning and opportunity can all matter.
nodes.sources: Steel (2007), nature of procrastination; Sirois & Pychyl (2013), procrastination and mood regulation.

nodes.title: Why the distinction matters
nodes.body:
The application may lack accessible instructions or contain genuinely unclear requirements that prevent Dev from starting.

lessons.title: Two explanations can sound reasonable
lessons.teach: Evidence should be able to change which explanation you prefer.
lessons.objective: Apply foundations to observable evidence, uncertainty and proportional decisions.

nodes.title: Start with competing accounts
nodes.body:
Starting the task triggers discomfort about producing an inadequate response. Avoiding the first step reduces that discomfort immediately, making delay tempting again.

Another possibility: The application may lack accessible instructions or contain genuinely unclear requirements that prevent Dev from starting.
nodes.sources: Steel (2007), nature of procrastination; Sirois & Pychyl (2013), procrastination and mood regulation.

nodes.title: What should we find out?
nodes.prompt: Both interpretations are plausible. What would actually help choose between them?
nodes.explanation: Test whether reducing the first step or clarifying expectations changes initiation while holding the goal constant. The question is what would change our view, rather than what would merely confirm it.
nodes.counterexample: Procrastination is not enough to establish laziness or a motivational deficit. Task demands, executive functioning and opportunity can all matter.
nodes.sources: Steel (2007), nature of procrastination; Sirois & Pychyl (2013), procrastination and mood regulation.

options.label: Ask the speakers how intense their feelings were and use the stronger reaction to identify the main cause.
options.feedback: The strength of a feeling does not establish its cause.

options.label: Ask for a longer account from the speaker who was most upset, since they experienced the largest impact.
options.feedback: The account matters, but the amount of distress is not a direct test of someone else’s motive.

options.label: Test whether reducing the first step or clarifying expectations changes initiation while holding the goal constant.
options.feedback: This observation could make a meaningful difference between the competing explanations.

options.label: Find a second argument and see whether it sounds similar without comparing what changed.
options.feedback: A similar argument can occur for different reasons; comparison requires the relevant circumstances.

options.label: Ask an uninvolved friend to guess which personality type best describes the speaker.
options.feedback: A personality guess is less useful than identifying a testable difference between the proposed processes.

nodes.title: Something new has been found
nodes.body: Dev completes the same form in fifteen minutes when a colleague sits beside him and asks him to write an imperfect first draft.
nodes.sources: Steel (2007), nature of procrastination; Sirois & Pychyl (2013), procrastination and mood regulation.

nodes.title: Revise your view
nodes.prompt: Which response to this new information is justified?
nodes.explanation: The rapid change suggests that initiation demands and evaluation concerns may contribute more than a lack of interest in the placement.
nodes.counterexample: Procrastination is not enough to establish laziness or a motivational deficit. Task demands, executive functioning and opportunity can all matter.
nodes.sources: Steel (2007), nature of procrastination; Sirois & Pychyl (2013), procrastination and mood regulation.

options.label: Keep the original explanation because it initially fitted the facts.
options.feedback: A reasonable earlier account can be revised as new evidence appears.

options.label: Prefer the explanation that most closely matches the new detail, while keeping other plausible causes open.
options.feedback: This revises confidence in response to information rather than to the apparent sophistication of the theory.

options.label: Treat the new evidence as decisive proof of a single hidden intention.
options.feedback: The evidence can favour an account without establishing complete access to another person’s motives.

options.label: Give every explanation identical weight because certainty is impossible.
options.feedback: Uncertainty does not require all accounts to be equally likely.

options.label: Ignore the new detail until each speaker independently agrees on its meaning.
options.feedback: Agreement may help cooperation, but it is not a prerequisite for evaluating evidence.

lessons.title: Ready for a real case
lessons.teach: You have the concepts. Now practise using them without jumping beyond the evidence.
lessons.objective: Apply foundations to observable evidence, uncertainty and proportional decisions.

lessons.title: The task behind the task
lessons.teach: Follow the conversation one message at a time. Notice what the behaviour might be achieving before you decide why it happened. About five minutes.
lessons.objective: Distinguish observable evidence from a tentative explanation of knowing what to do but not beginning.

nodes.title: Watch the conversation
nodes.prompt: Read the exchange one message at a time, then work from what the characters actually said.
nodes.sources: Steel (2007), procrastination; Sirois & Pychyl (2013), mood regulation.
nodes.scenario: Lena has the information for a grant application but has not drafted the difficult section.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: I know the deadline, but I can't bring myself to start.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Which bit feels hardest to approach?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Explaining why the idea deserves funding.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Have you tried a rough draft of that part?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: I keep reorganising my notes instead. At least that feels useful.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: What if you wrote two bad sentences nobody else has to see?

checks.prompt: Which psychological interpretation is currently best supported?

options.label: Lena may be using lower-stakes preparation to avoid exposing her proposal to evaluation.
Lena may lack the information required by the grant question.
Lena may have deliberately scheduled planning before writing.
Lena may be allocating time to organise notes because that work feels productive and offers clearer progress than drafting.
options.feedback: Preparation can be useful; its function changes if it repeatedly postpones the difficult section.

options.label: The practical constraint may be the largest contributor to this disagreement, with the emotional response emerging from frustration about the outcome.
options.feedback: This is a reasonable line of inquiry, although Lena may be using lower-stakes preparation to avoid exposing her proposal to evaluation. is more directly tied to the words in this scene. Difficulty starting can also reflect executive-function demands, unavailable resources or unclear instructions. One formulation will not fit everyone.

checks.explanation: The strongest clues are the character's own words. Lena may be using lower-stakes preparation to avoid exposing her proposal to evaluation. Lena may lack the information required by the grant question. remains a legitimate rival, so this is a working account rather than a conclusion about personality.
checks.counterexample: Difficulty starting can also reflect executive-function demands, unavailable resources or unclear instructions. One formulation will not fit everyone.

checks.prompt: You are Lena. Which response best addresses the practical problem at this point?

options.label: Speak an imperfect answer aloud and transcribe the useful parts before editing the wording.
options.consequence: This changes the starting format, although the written application still needs its own revision.
options.feedback: This changes the starting format, although the written application still needs its own revision.

options.label: Choose the hardest sentence in the section and draft a deliberately provisional version before reorganising the notes.
options.consequence: Directly engaging the avoided task may help, but the best first step may be smaller.
options.feedback: Directly engaging the avoided task may help, but the best first step may be smaller.

A student delays sending a routine email because choosing a subject line feels strangely difficult, then feels relief as soon as they close the draft.

nodes.title: An idea worth carrying forward
nodes.body:
Starting the task triggers discomfort about producing an inadequate response. Avoiding the first step reduces that discomfort immediately, making delay tempting again.

Procrastination is not enough to establish laziness or a motivational deficit. Task demands, executive functioning and opportunity can all matter.

The purpose of the exercise is to make a better-supported judgement and choose a proportionate next step.
nodes.sources: Steel (2007), nature of procrastination; Sirois & Pychyl (2013), procrastination and mood regulation.

glossary.definition: A person's willingness or reason to move towards a goal.
glossary.example: A student wants the placement and has already found the application form.
glossary.limit: Wanting the result does not guarantee that every step will feel easy.

glossary.definition: Anything about starting or doing an action that raises the effort needed.
glossary.example: An empty personal statement box feels too open-ended to begin.
glossary.limit: An apparently small task may have high demands for a particular person.

glossary.definition: The immediate easing of discomfort after stepping away from a difficult action.
glossary.example: Closing the form briefly stops the stress of writing a first sentence.
glossary.limit: Short-term relief can make delay more tempting, even when the deadline makes life harder.

glossary.definition: A deliberately manageable action that lowers the difficulty of beginning.
glossary.example: Write one rough sentence and keep it there for two minutes.
glossary.limit: The first action need not solve the whole task to make a useful difference.
